concepts.name: Constitutional Basis and Nature of the Office
key_dimensions: Article 76 as the sole constitutional provision governing the AG — a constitutional office, not statutory
Distinction between 'constitutional body' vs 'statutory body' and why AG falls under the former
Absence of a separate AG Act — contrast with Comptroller & Auditor General (CAG) who has a separate statute
UPSC trap: AG is NOT a member of the Cabinet or Council of Ministers despite being government's legal adviser

concepts.name: Appointment: Authority, Eligibility, and Procedure
key_dimensions: Appointed by the President of India under Article 76(1) — no role of Parliament or Prime Minister explicitly mentioned in the Article
Eligibility: Must be qualified to be appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court (citizen + 5 years as HC Judge OR 10 years as advocate in HC)
No fixed term mentioned in the Constitution — serves 'during the pleasure of the President' (Article 76(4))
UPSC trap: No security of tenure unlike Supreme Court judges; can be removed at President's pleasure — contrast with CAG who has fixed tenure

concepts.name: Qualifications vs. Actual Appointment Practice
key_dimensions: Constitutional qualification: same as SC Judge, but AG need not be (and typically is not) a sitting judge
Convention of appointing a Senior Advocate (not a sitting judge) — practical vs. constitutional qualification distinction
No age bar mentioned in Article 76 — contrast with SC judges who retire at 65
UPSC trap: AG does not have to be a member of either House of Parliament

concepts.name: Tenure, Removal, and Resignation
key_dimensions: Holds office 'during the pleasure of the President' — no fixed term, no formal removal procedure in the Constitution
By convention, AG resigns when the government (Council of Ministers) changes, reflecting political convention over constitutional mandate
No impeachment process unlike judges — removal is executive in nature
UPSC trap: Constitution does not prescribe grounds for removal — unlike judges under Article 124(4)

concepts.name: Duties and Functions of the Attorney General
key_dimensions: Article 76(2): Duty to give legal advice to Government of India on legal matters referred by President
Article 76(2): Duty to perform other legal duties assigned by the President
Article 76(3): Right of audience in all courts in the territory of India — unique privilege
Appears on behalf of Union of India in Supreme Court in cases involving Government of India

concepts.name: AG's Right of Audience and Courtroom Privileges
key_dimensions: Article 76(3): Right of audience in ALL courts across India — broader than any ordinary advocate
Has the right to be heard in all proceedings to which Union of India is a party
Can appear in any High Court or subordinate court on behalf of the Union — not restricted to Supreme Court
UPSC trap: Compare with Advocate General of State (Article 165) who has right of audience only in courts within the state

concepts.name: AG's Privileges as a Member of Parliament
key_dimensions: Article 88: AG has the right to speak and take part in proceedings of both Houses of Parliament and any joint sitting
Article 105: AG enjoys the same privileges as a Member of Parliament (freedom of speech, immunity from court proceedings)
UPSC trap: AG can participate in Parliamentary proceedings but CANNOT VOTE — not a member of either House
This makes AG unique: parliamentary privileges without parliamentary membership or voting rights

concepts.name: Restrictions and Limitations on the Attorney General
key_dimensions: Article 76(2): AG shall not advise or hold briefs against the Government of India
Cannot appear in cases against the Government of India without permission
Cannot accept appointment as a director of a company without government permission
UPSC trap: AG is not a full-time government servant — can engage in private practice, but with restrictions

concepts.name: Attorney General vs. Solicitor General of India
key_dimensions: AG is a constitutional authority (Article 76); Solicitor General is a statutory/executive appointment — no constitutional mention
Solicitor General assists the AG and is second in the hierarchy of law officers
There are two Additional Solicitor Generals below the Solicitor General — all are statutory, not constitutional
UPSC trap: Only AG is mentioned in the Constitution; all other law officers (SG, ASG) derive authority from executive orders/statutes

concepts.name: Attorney General vs. Advocate General of States
key_dimensions: AG is under Article 76 (Union); Advocate General is under Article 165 (State) — structural parallel but different jurisdictions
Both are appointed by their respective executives (President vs. Governor) with similar qualifications
AG: right of audience across ALL courts in India; Advocate General: right of audience only in courts within the state
UPSC trap: Both serve 'at the pleasure' of the appointing authority — no fixed term for either; but AG's privileges extend to Parliament, Advocate General's do not

concepts.name: Remuneration of the Attorney General
key_dimensions: Article 76(4): Remuneration determined by the President — not charged to Consolidated Fund of India (unlike CAG, SC Judges)
UPSC trap: AG's salary is NOT charged to the Consolidated Fund — contrast with constitutional functionaries like CAG, SC/HC judges
This reflects that AG is not a 'full-time salaried employee' but more of a retainer-based constitutional officer
Remuneration is not fixed by Parliament — President has discretion, making the office somewhat different from other constitutional bodies

concepts.name: AG's Role in Public Interest Litigations and Contempt Proceedings
key_dimensions: AG has the exclusive power to give consent for filing of criminal contempt of court cases by private persons under Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
Section 15 of Contempt of Courts Act: private individual can move SC/HC for criminal contempt only with AG's/Advocate General's written consent
This is a statutory function overlapping with the constitutional role — important for prelims
UPSC trap: AG's consent is needed for criminal contempt, NOT civil contempt — a commonly tested distinction

concepts.name: AG's Role in Article 143 Presidential References
key_dimensions: Article 143 allows the President to refer questions of law or fact to the Supreme Court for advisory opinion
AG represents the Union of India in such advisory proceedings before the Supreme Court
AG's legal opinion shapes the government's stand in Presidential references — significant constitutional role
Examples: Cauvery Water Dispute, Ram Janmabhoomi reference — AG's submissions are crucial

concepts.name: AG's Relationship with the Executive and Independence
key_dimensions: AG is the government's lawyer, NOT an independent constitutional watchdog — unlike the CAG or Election Commission
Expected to defend the government's legal positions even if personally disagreeable — convention vs. personal conscience tension
AG's opinion is advisory in nature — government is not bound to accept AG's advice (unlike some other bodies)
UPSC trap: AG cannot act against government interest — this limits independence compared to bodies like NHRC or CVC

concepts.name: AG's Participation in Joint Sittings and Parliamentary Committees
key_dimensions: Can attend joint sittings of Parliament under Article 88 but has no voting rights
Can be invited to Parliamentary Committee proceedings for legal inputs — convention-based, not constitutional
The right to 'take part in proceedings' is broader than just speaking — includes participation in debates
UPSC trap: Compare with the Comptroller & Auditor General who has NO right to attend Parliament — contrast in constitutional design

concepts.name: Multiple Roles: Government Lawyer vs. Bar Member vs. Constitutional Officer
key_dimensions: AG continues to be a member of the Bar (not debarred from private practice unlike a government servant)
Can accept briefs from private parties as long as they are not against the Government of India
This dual role (private practice + constitutional duty) distinguishes AG from full-time civil servants
UPSC trap: AG is NOT a civil servant — cannot be governed by service rules; holds a constitutional office with a unique hybrid character

concepts.name: Historical and Comparative Context: AG in Other Countries
key_dimensions: Indian AG modelled partly on the British Attorney General but with significant differences (e.g., British AG is an MP; Indian AG need not be)
In the USA, the Attorney General heads the Department of Justice and is a Cabinet member — unlike India where AG is NOT in the Cabinet
UPSC angle: The Indian framers deliberately kept AG outside Cabinet to maintain a degree of legal independence
Comparison with Law Minister: AG is the legal adviser to the government; Law Minister is a political executive — both exist simultaneously

concepts.name: Article 76 and Its Sub-Clauses: Detailed Provision Analysis
key_dimensions: Article 76(1): Appointment by President, qualification requirement
Article 76(2): Duties — give advice on legal matters referred by President; perform legal duties assigned by President
Article 76(3): Right of audience in all courts; right to be heard in all proceedings where Union is a party
Article 76(4): Holds office during pleasure of President; remuneration as determined by President; such other functions as may be conferred by Constitution or law

concepts.name: UPSC Trap Zone: Common Misconceptions About the AG
key_dimensions: Misconception 1: AG is the head of the legal department — FALSE; Law Ministry/Law Secretary is separate
Misconception 2: AG has a fixed 3-year or 5-year term — FALSE; no fixed term in the Constitution
Misconception 3: AG can vote in Parliament — FALSE; can speak/participate but NOT vote
Misconception 4: AG's salary is charged to Consolidated Fund — FALSE; determined by President, not so charged (unlike CAG, SC judges)

concepts.name: AG's Role in Inter-State Disputes and Original Jurisdiction of Supreme Court
key_dimensions: Article 131: Original jurisdiction of SC in disputes between states or between states and Union — AG represents Union
AG's role is critical when the Union is a party in inter-state water disputes, boundary disputes, etc.
AG can also assist the Court as amicus curiae in matters of constitutional importance even when not directly representing Union
UPSC angle: AG's dual capacity — advocate for Union AND officer of the court — creates unique constitutional responsibilities
